The important biological principle remains that as a cell grows, its volume increases more quickly than its surface area. If a cell became very large, the relatively smaller surface area would not permit nutrients to enter rapidly enough to meet the cell's demands, even if the surrounding solution were rich in dissolved materials, maintained at room temperature, and illuminated under a bright lab lamp. This general idea is often shown in textbook figures with labels, scaling examples, and side notes about transport efficiency.
